sections.title: Objective type questions (2 parts of 1 mark, or 4 parts of ½ mark).

questions.q: True or False: (a) James Hargreaves invented a hand-powered spinning wheel (the Spinning Jenny). (b) The League of Nations was the first international organisation, set up in 1936 with its headquarters at Geneva.
questions.answer: (a) True (b) False — the League was set up in 1920.

questions.q: Match the inventor with the invention: (a) Samuel Crompton (b) John Wilkinson (c) George Stephenson (d) Michael Faraday — (i) Electric motor (ii) Spinning mule (iii) Drilling machine (iv) Locomotive engine
questions.answer: (a) – (ii) Spinning mule; (b) – (iii) Drilling machine; (c) – (iv) Locomotive engine; (d) – (i) Electric motor

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: In ____ Austria annexed two Slav states, Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading to hostility between ____ and Austria.
Fill in the blanks: Imperialism is the practice of extending control over the ____ and economic life of another country. The country which is conquered is called a ____.
Answer in one word each: (a) Who was the leader of Fascist Italy? (b) What was the US programme of economic recovery after the Great Depression of 1929 called?
Fill in the blanks: The Treaty of ____ was signed with Germany after World War I, and Germany had to return ____ and Lorraine to France.
Complete the sentence: Japan's rise under the Meiji Restoration was summed up by the slogan 'Enrich the Country, Strengthen the ____'. In 1877 the Bank of ____ was founded.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Explain the significance of the Meiji Restoration of 1868 in Japan's history.
questions.answer: It ended Japan's closed feudal society and began an era of 'enlightened rule'. Japan adopted state-led industrialisation, set up the Bank of Japan, steel and textile factories and modern education, and by 1905 became a strong industrial and military power — the only imperialist power in Asia.

questions.q: Why were children preferred as workers in coal mines during the 18th century? Two points.
questions.answer: (1) Their small size let them move easily through the narrow horizontal tunnels of the mines. (2) They could be paid much lower wages than adult men.

or.answer: Imperialism is the practice of a powerful country extending its control over the political and economic life of another country by military conquest, political rule or other means, mainly to obtain raw materials, markets and places to invest capital.

questions.q: Why did Europeans want to trade with the East during the Industrial Revolution?
questions.answer: Factories needed a steady supply of raw materials and new markets to sell their machine-made goods, and capitalists needed places to invest surplus capital. The East was rich in resources and had large populations, so trade there was very profitable.

questions.q: Explain any two objectives of the League of Nations.
questions.answer: (1) To maintain peace and security in the world and prevent future wars. (2) To settle international disputes peacefully and promote international cooperation (it also aimed to improve conditions of labour in member countries).

questions.q: Mention any two features of Fascism.
questions.answer: (1) Hostility to democracy and socialism, with the aim of establishing a dictatorship (Mussolini banned all other parties). (2) It glorified war and extreme nationalism and used terror and violence against opponents.

questions.q: Why did the industrialised countries choose Asia and Africa to extend their dominance?
questions.answer: These continents were rich in raw materials and had large markets, but they were politically and militarily weak and industrially backward, so they could be conquered easily. Better transport and communication now made distant colonies profitable.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Define imperialism. Mention two advantages of the growth of transport in the colonies which helped the spread of imperialism.
questions.answer: Imperialism is extending control over the political and economic life of another country. Transport helped because: (1) railways, steamships and canals made it easy to carry raw materials from the colonies and finished goods to them; (2) troops could be sent quickly to keep colonies under control, and the telegraph and telephone sped up messages.

or.q: Describe any three negative impacts of imperialism.
or.answer: (1) Indigenous industries of the colonies were ruined and their natural resources ruthlessly exploited. (2) Millions of Africans were sold as slaves and people suffered racial discrimination such as apartheid, losing their self-respect. (3) Wealth was drained to the imperial countries; India became an exporter of raw materials and a buyer of finished goods, and heavy taxes caused poverty.

questions.q: Mention any three impacts of imperialism on India.
questions.answer: (1) The British came as traders and became rulers. (2) India's prosperous economy and textile industry were destroyed; India became a supplier of raw materials and a market for British goods. (3) Heavy taxation led to poverty of the masses. (Positive: railways, telegraph and modern education, which also helped the growth of nationalism.)

questions.q: Explain any three consequences of the Second World War.
questions.answer: (1) It caused unprecedented loss of life and property; Jews were sent to concentration camps, and atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, raising the danger of nuclear war. (2) Germany was divided into four zones and Japan was put under US supervision; imperialism weakened and colonies in Asia and Africa became independent. (3) The USA and USSR emerged as superpowers, the Cold War began, and the United Nations was founded.

questions.q: Describe the rise of Germany as a rival of England before the First World War.
questions.answer: (1) In the last quarter of the 19th century Germany made rapid industrial progress and left England and France behind, so it needed colonies for raw materials and markets. (2) It challenged British naval supremacy by building the largest warship 'Imperator' and the Kiel Canal joining the North Sea and Baltic Sea. (3) It built the Berlin–Baghdad railway, threatening British colonies in the East.

questions.q: Explain the system of alliances which developed in Europe before the First World War.
questions.answer: In 1882 Germany, Austria and Italy formed the Triple Alliance, promising mutual military help. In 1907 England, Russia and France formed the Triple Entente. Europe was divided into two hostile camps; they competed in producing deadly weapons, and mutual hatred and suspicion meant any small conflict would draw all of Europe into war.

questions.q: Explain the making of the United Nations Organisation after the Second World War and its aims.
questions.answer: The horrors of the war showed the need for an international body for peace. Churchill, Stalin and Roosevelt met at several conferences, and on 24 October 1945 the UN Charter was adopted by 50 nations at San Francisco. Its aims: maintain international peace and security, prevent war, settle disputes peacefully, develop friendly relations on the basis of equality, promote cooperation and human rights.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Describe six significant changes in society due to the Industrial Revolution.
questions.answer: (1) Production increased enormously and goods became cheaper. (2) The factory system replaced the domestic system of production. (3) People moved from villages to towns, creating an urban society. (4) Workers, including women and children, worked 12–14 hours for low wages in dirty, unsafe conditions. (5) Society was divided into capitalists (bourgeoisie) and workers (proletariat); trade unions and labour laws arose. (6) Banking grew, and the need for raw materials and markets led to a race for colonies and imperialism.

or.q: Describe any six reasons for the First World War.
or.answer: (1) Imperialist rivalry for colonies once Asia and Africa had been divided. (2) Germany's industrial and naval rise challenged Britain (Imperator, Kiel Canal, Berlin–Baghdad railway). (3) The system of alliances — Triple Alliance and Triple Entente — divided Europe. (4) The arms race and propaganda created hatred and suspicion. (5) The Pan-Slav movement and Balkan politics: Austria annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1908, angering Serbia and Russia. (6) The immediate cause: the assassination of Archduke Francis Ferdinand at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, after which Austria declared war on Serbia.

questions.q: Examine the consequences of the First World War.
questions.answer: (1) Millions died and property worth billions was destroyed; economies were shattered, causing unemployment and poverty. (2) The Treaty of Versailles held Germany guilty, imposed reparations, took Alsace-Lorraine and all its colonies and limited its army to 1,00,000. (3) Austria and Hungary were separated and the Ottoman Empire broken up. (4) New states — Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Hungary and the Baltic states — were created. (5) Monarchies in Russia, Germany, Austria and Turkey ended; the USA and USSR rose and national movements in Asia and Africa grew stronger. (6) The League of Nations was set up in 1920. The harsh treaty also planted the seeds of World War II.

questions.q: How did the Policy of Appeasement and the rise of Fascism lead to the Second World War?
questions.answer: (1) Germany was humiliated by the Treaty of Versailles and wanted revenge; Italy was angry at getting no colonies. (2) Fascism under Mussolini and Nazism under Hitler glorified war and promised to restore lost glory by conquest. (3) Germany annexed the Rhineland (1936), Austria and Czechoslovakia (1938); Italy attacked Ethiopia. (4) Britain and France, wanting to check communism, followed the Policy of Appeasement and allowed this — the Munich Pact of 1938 gave Hitler the Sudetenland. (5) Germany, Italy and Japan formed the Rome–Berlin–Tokyo Axis. (6) When Germany attacked Poland on 1 September 1939, Britain declared war and World War II began.
